title: Mutation testing and test quality
description: Use mutation testing to measure how effective your React tests really are and identify the gaps that traditional coverage metrics miss.

data.text: Code coverage is a widely used metric, but it measures only whether a line was executed — not whether a test would catch a bug if that line changed. Mutation testing fills this gap. It introduces small, deliberate bugs (mutations) into your code and then checks whether your test suite catches them. If a mutant survives, it means your tests have a blind spot.

For a senior frontend engineer, mutation testing is a powerful tool for evaluating the quality of a React test suite, particularly for complex components with conditional logic, event handlers, and derived state.
A mutation testing tool takes your source code, applies a set of mutation operators, and runs your tests against each mutated version. Common mutation operators include:

items: Remove a conditional branch (replace an if body with an empty block)
Replace a return value with a literal (true, 0, or an empty string)

data.text: If your tests pass on the mutated code, the mutant survived. If they fail, the mutant was killed. A high mutation score means your tests are sensitive to real changes in behavior.
Example: a component with hidden mutation risk

Consider a button component that disables itself while a form submits. A superficial test might render the component and check the label, but never exercise the disabled state. Here is the component and a test that looks complete but has a low mutation score:

data.caption: SubmitButton component and a weak test that misses the disabled-state mutation
Stronger test that kills the disabled-state mutation
data.code:
// ✅ Strong test: exercises both states
render(<SubmitButton isSubmitting={false} onClick={vi.fn()} />)
expect(screen.getByRole('button')).toHaveTextContent('Submit')
expect(screen.getByRole('button')).not.toBeDisabled()

render(<SubmitButton isSubmitting={true} onClick={vi.fn()} />)
expect(screen.getByRole('button')).toHaveTextContent('Submitting...')
expect(screen.getByRole('button')).toBeDisabled()

data.text: A mutation testing tool would kill the first test immediately: when the disabled prop is removed from the source, the weak test still passes. The second test fails, meaning the mutation was caught.
Running mutation testing in a React project
Stryker is the most widely used mutation testing tool for TypeScript and React. It integrates with Vitest and can run as part of your CI pipeline. A typical workflow is:

items: Install Stryker and configure it for Vitest.
Run Stryker on a small, high-value subset of components first — do not mutate the entire codebase on day one.
Review surviving mutants and add targeted assertions to kill them.
Set a minimum mutation score threshold (e.g., 80%) in CI so regressions are blocked.

data.title: Practical limits
data.text: Mutation testing is compute-intensive. Do not run it on every commit. Run it nightly or on a schedule, and focus on components with complex logic: forms, data tables, and state machines. Simple presentational components are unlikely to benefit as much.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: Code coverage measures execution, not bug-catching ability.
Mutation testing reveals test blind spots that coverage cannot.
A surviving mutant is a signal to add a targeted assertion, not to delete the component.
Use mutation testing as a quality audit tool, not a gate for every PR.
